name: The Social Contract
statement: Governments are legitimate only by the consent of the governed, as if founded on an agreement among them.
statementAccent: as if founded on an agreement among them
meaning: The social contract is the central idea of a tradition in political philosophy holding that people's moral and political obligations depend on an agreement among them to form the society in which they live, so that legitimate political authority derives from the consent of the governed rather than from divine right or natural hierarchy. The contract may be understood as an actual or, more often, a hypothetical agreement by which individuals give up some freedoms in exchange for the security and benefits of organized society and government. The idea was developed by the great modern social contract theorists, who differed sharply. Thomas Hobbes, in Leviathan of 1651, argued that in the state of nature life would be a war of all against all, solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short, so people rationally surrender their rights to an absolute sovereign for the sake of peace and security. John Locke held that people possess natural rights to life, liberty, and property, and that government exists by consent to protect those rights and may be overthrown if it fails. Jean-Jacques Rousseau, in The Social Contract of 1762, argued that legitimate authority rests on the general will of the people. The social contract remains foundational to modern political thought, liberalism, and democratic theory.
mechanism: Social contract theory reasons about the origins and justification of political authority by imagining what people would agree to. It typically begins from a hypothetical starting point, a state of nature without government, and asks what rational individuals in that condition would consent to in order to escape its problems and secure the benefits of society. The agreement they would reach, the social contract, then serves to justify the state and to set the terms and limits of its authority. Because the parties are imagined to agree, the resulting political order is grounded in consent rather than force, and its legitimacy depends on whether it serves the purposes for which people would have agreed to it. The major theorists reach different conclusions because they picture human nature and the state of nature differently. Hobbes, seeing the state of nature as a terrifying war of all against all, argues that people would agree to an absolute sovereign whose power is nearly unlimited, since any government is better than chaos. Locke, seeing the state of nature as governed by natural law but lacking an impartial judge, argues for a limited government by consent that protects natural rights and can be resisted if it betrays its trust. Rousseau argues that the people themselves, acting through the general will, are the sovereign, so legitimate law is self-given. The device of the contract thus links human nature, consent, and the proper form and limits of government.

examples.text: Hobbes argued that to escape a war of all against all, people would surrender their rights to an absolute sovereign for security.
Locke held that government exists by consent to protect natural rights and may be overthrown if it fails that trust.
Rousseau argued that legitimate authority rests on the general will, so the sovereign people give themselves their own laws.

variants.name: Hobbes, Locke, and Rousseau
variants.text: The three great modern theorists, who agreed the contract grounds authority but disagreed on human nature and the form of government.

variants.name: Rawls's revival
variants.text: John Rawls's twentieth-century revival, replacing the state of nature with the original position behind a veil of ignorance.

whyItMatters: The social contract is one of the most influential ideas in the history of political philosophy, because it grounds the legitimacy of government in the consent of the governed rather than in divine right, tradition, or brute force. By imagining political authority as arising from an agreement among free individuals, social contract theory provided a powerful framework for asking when a government is justified, what it owes its citizens, and when it may rightfully be resisted, and it became the intellectual foundation of modern liberalism and democratic theory. The differing accounts of Hobbes, Locke, and Rousseau shaped competing visions of the state, from absolute sovereignty to limited government to popular sovereignty, and their ideas directly influenced the great political revolutions, with Locke informing the American Declaration of Independence and Rousseau the French Revolution. In the twentieth century, John Rawls revived the tradition to address questions of justice. The concepts of consent, rights, and legitimacy that the social contract introduced remain central to how modern societies think about political authority and its limits.

working.text: start from a hypothetical state of nature to ask what people would agree to in order to leave it.
determine what rational individuals would consent to for the security and benefits of organized society.
treat the resulting contract as the source and limit of legitimate political authority.

limits: The social contract is a powerful device but carries well-known difficulties. No literal historical contract was ever signed, so for most theorists it is a hypothetical or tacit agreement rather than a real event, and critics from Hume onward have questioned whether the tacit consent supposed to bind people who merely live under a government is genuine consent at all. The tradition has also been criticized for whom it left out: Carole Pateman argued that the classic social contract presupposed a prior sexual contract subordinating women, and Charles Mills argued that an underlying racial contract defined who counted as a full person and excluded non-white peoples, so the ostensibly universal agreement was in practice exclusionary. The differing accounts of Hobbes, Locke, and Rousseau reach opposite conclusions, showing that the device's results depend heavily on assumptions about human nature.
misreadings: The social contract is not a claim that people literally signed an agreement to form government; for most theorists it is a hypothetical or tacit device for justifying authority, and whether tacit consent is real consent is itself disputed. It does not yield a single political conclusion, since Hobbes, Locke, and Rousseau derived absolutism, limited government, and popular sovereignty from it. And its ostensibly universal agreement was in practice exclusionary, as feminist and racial critiques note, so treating the contract as a real historical event, as pointing to one form of government, or as genuinely universal, misreads a hypothetical and contested framework for political legitimacy.
origin: The central idea of the social contract tradition in political philosophy, developed by Hobbes in 1651, Locke, and Rousseau in 1762 and revived by Rawls, grounding legitimate government in the consent of the governed.
